Lagging vs leading.long:
A lagging indicator summarises what price has already done — a moving average is the plainest case. A leading indicator claims to signal what price is about to do. The distinction is standard vocabulary, and it smuggles in a large claim.

Every indicator computed from price alone is lagging in the strict sense, because its inputs are completed bars. The ones marketed as leading — oscillators, divergence readings — are transformations of the same past data, reframed so that certain configurations tend to appear near turns. Appearing near turns in hindsight is not the same as signalling turns in advance, since the same configurations also appear mid-trend, where acting on them is expensive.

Genuinely leading information exists, but it lives outside the chart: scheduled data releases, earnings dates, known flows. Those lead because they are causes, not summaries.

Where people get fooled: buying the label. Calling an oscillator leading does not give it foresight; it describes the hope, not the mechanism. The honest question for any indicator is what it computes and from what inputs — an answer that is always some arrangement of past prices.
Lagging vs leading.usage: Generally used to classify indicators; the classification flatters oscillators, which are transformations of past price like everything else.

Moving average.long:
A moving average is the mean of the last N closes, recalculated each bar. It smooths the series so the drift is visible under the noise, at the cost of arriving late: the average contains only completed bars, so it turns after price turns, by roughly half its window.

That lag is not a flaw to engineer away — it is the price of smoothing, and every variant (exponential, weighted, hull) trades a little lag for a little more twitchiness. The average also gives a workable definition of trend for systematic rules: price above a rising average is as good a one-line trend filter as exists, not because the line has power but because it restates the drift.

The popular windows — 20, 50, 200 — are conventions. Nothing in the market cares about them beyond the extent to which other participants watch the same lines, which for the 200-day on major indices is a real but modest effect.

Where people get fooled: treating the average as support, as if the line itself holds price. Price interacts with the levels where orders rest; the average passes through such levels constantly, and takes credit when it does.
Moving average.usage: Typically used as a trend filter or smoothing device; the window choice is a convention, and the lag is the cost of the smoothing.

RSI.long:
The Relative Strength Index, published by J. Welles Wilder in 1978, compares average gains to average losses over a window — 14 periods by default — and scales the result between 0 and 100. High readings mean recent bars have been mostly up; low readings, mostly down.

That is the entire content: RSI is a normalised summary of recent momentum. The conventional 70/30 lines, marked overbought and oversold, add an interpretation the arithmetic does not support — that stretched momentum implies reversal. In ranging markets the interpretation works passably, because prices oscillate; in trends it is expensive, because a strong trend holds the RSI stretched for weeks while the mean-reversion trader repeatedly fades it.

So the indicator's meaning depends entirely on a regime the indicator itself cannot detect. Whatever decides ranging from trending is doing the real work, and that judgement comes from somewhere else.

Where people get fooled: reading 70 as a sell signal in itself. Overbought describes the recent past, not a force acting on the future — the most overbought markets are the strongest ones, which is precisely when fading them costs the most.
RSI.usage: Generally used as a momentum oscillator with 70/30 conventions; its readings mean opposite things in ranges and trends.

MACD.long:
The MACD, developed by Gerald Appel, subtracts a 26-period exponential moving average from a 12-period one, then smooths that difference with a 9-period signal line. Crossovers, the histogram between the lines, and the zero line are the standard readings.

Unpacked, it is the gap between two smoothed versions of price — a measure of whether the shorter-run drift is outrunning the longer-run drift. That makes it a momentum gauge built from moving averages, inheriting their lag twice over. The crossovers translate to: recent momentum has changed relative to slightly less recent momentum, some bars ago.

As a descriptive tool on higher timeframes it is serviceable — the histogram shrinking during a rally is a compact way to see the advance decelerating. As a signal generator its crossovers whipsaw in exactly the conditions that produce most bars: sideways markets, where the two averages braid around each other.

Where people get fooled: the three-part construction — two lines, a histogram, named parameters — reads as sophistication, but 12, 26 and 9 are conventions from a different market era, and varying them mostly demonstrates how much the output depends on arbitrary inputs.
MACD.usage: Typically read via signal-line crossovers and histogram momentum; it is a lag-on-lag construction, best treated as description.

Bollinger Bands.long:
Bollinger Bands, from John Bollinger, plot a 20-period moving average with bands two standard deviations either side. The bands widen when recent bars have been volatile and tighten when they have been quiet, so the envelope is a rolling picture of volatility around trend.

Two honest uses follow directly. The band width measures volatility compression — the squeeze — which matters because quiet periods tend to precede expansions, though the direction of the expansion is not indicated. And a close far outside the bands states that the current bar is statistically unusual against the recent past, which is worth knowing regardless of what you do about it.

The dishonest use is mechanical: sell the upper band, buy the lower. In a trend, price walks along one band for extended stretches, and the touch that looked like an extreme was simply the trend proceeding.

Where people get fooled: the two-standard-deviation dressing implies price should stay inside the bands 95 percent of the time. That figure assumes returns are normally distributed and independent, and they are neither — band walks and gap-throughs are far more common than the statistics costume suggests.
Bollinger Bands.usage: Generally used to read volatility compression and expansion; band touches are information about recent dispersion, not signals in themselves.

ATR.long:
Average True Range, another Wilder design from 1978, measures how much an instrument typically moves per bar. True range is the largest of: high minus low, high minus prior close, low minus prior close — the third terms catching gaps — averaged over 14 periods by default.

ATR predicts nothing and does not try to. It answers a sizing question: how far does this market ordinarily travel in one bar? That answer feeds the most defensible uses any indicator has. A stop placed some multiple of ATR away is fitted to the instrument's actual noise rather than to a round number or a pain threshold. A position sized from that stop distance risks the same dollars whether the market is quiet or wild. Comparing ATR across instruments puts their movement on one scale.

Because every input is a completed bar, ATR lags volatility shifts — it understates risk in the first bars of a new regime, which is exactly when the understatement hurts.

Where people get fooled: using a calm-period ATR through an event. The stop calibrated to yesterday's quiet is one bar of news away from being inside the noise, and the position sized from it is suddenly twice as risky as intended.
ATR.usage: Typically used for stop placement and volatility-scaled position sizing — measurement rather than prediction, which is why it ages well.

Stochastic.long:
The stochastic oscillator, associated with George Lane, locates the latest close within the recent high-low range: 100 means closing at the top of the range, 0 at the bottom. A smoothed %K line and its %D signal average generate the standard crossover readings, with 80/20 as the overbought and oversold conventions.

The question it answers is narrow: where in the recent range are we closing? In a genuine range that is useful positional information — closes rotating from one extreme to the other is what a range is. The oscillator simply restates it at the cost of two smoothing choices.

In a trend the reading degenerates. Closing repeatedly near the top of the recent range is the definition of an uptrend, so the stochastic pins high and stays there, generating sell readings all the way up. Like every bounded oscillator, its interpretation depends on a regime call it cannot make itself.

Where people get fooled: crossovers in the extreme zones look precise and fire constantly, and in a range enough of them work to build faith. The same habits carried into a trend produce a long series of small losses that the earlier range period trained the trader to sit through.
Stochastic.usage: Generally used for range-position and crossover readings with 80/20 conventions; a range tool that keeps firing in trends.

Fibonacci retracement.long:
The Fibonacci retracement tool divides a completed swing into levels — 23.6, 38.2, 50, 61.8, 78.6 percent — and watches pullbacks for reactions at them. It is among the most used drawing tools in retail charting.

The premise, that ratios from the Fibonacci sequence govern pullback depth, has no documented mechanism. The defensible residue is smaller: pullbacks of every depth occur; shallow ones suggest a strong trend and deep ones a doubtful one; and pre-marking some levels gives a plan for where to act instead of improvising. Whether the marks sit at 38.2 or 40 percent changes little — the discipline of pre-commitment does the work the ratios get credit for.

There is also a modest self-fulfilling channel: enough traders drawing identical retracements from obvious swings put resting orders near the same prices, which can produce small genuine reactions in watched markets.

Where people get fooled: the anchor. Drawn from a different swing high or low, every level moves, and redrawing until a level lines up with what price already did is the standard way the tool convinces its users. Five levels, flexible anchoring and generous tolerance means something always appears to work.
Fibonacci retracement.usage: Typically drawn over a completed swing to frame pullback entries; the pre-commitment is the value, the specific ratios mostly are not.

Divergence.long:
Divergence is a disagreement between price and an oscillator: price makes a new high while the RSI or MACD makes a lower high, or price a new low while the oscillator holds above its prior low. It is read as momentum failing to confirm the move, hinting at exhaustion.

The observation is real — final legs of trends often do arrive with less momentum, and the oscillator, being a momentum summary, records that. The trouble is timing and base rate. Trends in progress generate divergences continuously: every pause after a strong leg prints one, and strong trends can carry a dozen successive divergences before anything reverses. The signal identifies a condition that is common within trends and only occasionally terminal.

Used descriptively — this advance is slowing — divergence is honest. Used as a standing reversal trigger, it amounts to repeatedly fading a trend because it decelerated, which is a losing habit in any persistent move.

Where people get fooled: hindsight selection. The divergence at the actual top is vivid in review; the eight before it, which resolved by the trend continuing, leave no trace in memory. Counting only the last one makes the tool look far sharper than its full record.
Divergence.usage: Generally read as momentum failing to confirm price; common within healthy trends, so it describes deceleration more than it times reversal.

Confluence.long:
Confluence is the stacking of multiple supporting factors at one price or moment — a retracement level meeting a prior high, a moving average and a round number — on the reasoning that several weak signals agree into a strong one.

The reasoning holds only if the signals are independent. Most chart-derived factors are not: the moving average, the retracement level and the old high are all computed from the same price series, and in a pullback they crowd into the same area automatically. Their agreement is near-guaranteed by construction, and adding a third correlated echo of the same information adds little that the first did not.

Genuine confluence — price-based reasons meeting something from outside price, like a scheduled event or documented positioning — is rarer and more interesting, precisely because the sources are independent.

Where people get fooled: confluence is unlimited in hindsight. With enough indicators available, any level that later mattered can be shown to have had five reasons, because five of the hundreds of things drawable through it can always be found. The honest test is to specify the required factors first and log every occurrence — including the confluent levels that price ignored entirely.
Confluence.usage: Typically invoked when several factors align at one level; alignment among price-derived factors is mostly automatic, not evidential.

Anchored VWAP.long:
Anchored VWAP is the volume-weighted average price measured from a chosen starting bar — an earnings release, a swing low, a high-volume session — rather than from the day's open. Every share traded since the anchor is averaged, weighted by volume, giving the mean price paid by everyone who transacted since that event.

That number has genuine meaning. If price sits above the VWAP anchored at an event, the average participant since the event is in profit; below, at a loss. Aggregate profit and loss shapes behaviour — trapped buyers supply resistance as price returns to their break-even — so the anchored line is a mechanically-motivated reference in a way most drawn lines are not.

The weakness is the anchor choice. Anchored from a different event, the line moves, and the freedom to pick anchors after the fact reintroduces the same flexibility that undermines retracement tools. One trader's meaningful event is another's arbitrary bar.

Where people get fooled: treating the line as support in itself. It marks where the average participant breaks even, which matters only insofar as those participants act there — thin markets, old anchors and small events produce lines nobody is defending.
Anchored VWAP.usage: Generally anchored at significant events to track the average price paid since; the mechanism is real, the anchor choice is the discretion.
